edges.description: Trophozoites that reach neural tissue attach to and ingest host cells with amoebastome food cups.
Trophozoites that have reached target tissues also release virulence factors and extracellular vesicles that injure host cells without direct phagocytic contact.
Amebae moving through the olfactory neuroepithelium and olfactory nerves can disrupt early smell perception as they cross toward the olfactory bulb.
Contact cytotoxicity contributes to the tissue destruction and necrosis of PAM.
Secreted vesicles and proteases add contact-independent epithelial and neural injury to the direct trophozoite cytotoxic mechanisms driving PAM tissue necrosis.
Matrix degradation facilitates movement from nasal chambers toward the olfactory bulb, enabling subsequent CNS invasion.
IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and other inflammatory mediators released by activated CNS innate immune cells provide a route from local trophozoite sensing to fever.
Microglial cytokine and oxidant release can add immunopathologic injury to direct amoebic cytolysis.
Necrotizing meningoencephalitis produces destructive edema that can raise intracranial pressure and progress to herniation.
Meningoencephalitic inflammation and edema generate severe headache during the acute CNS phase.
Acute meningoencephalitis and intracranial-pressure elevation account for the frequent vomiting-predominant presentation.
Meningeal inflammation produces meningismus and neck stiffness.
Diffuse necrotizing encephalitis disrupts cortical and subcortical function, producing encephalopathy.
Necrotizing cortical inflammation and edema lower the seizure threshold in fulminant PAM.
The acute CNS inflammatory response spills into CSF as neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis.
Brain swelling, herniation, and brainstem compression explain the rapid transition from meningoencephalitis to coma in advanced PAM.
Trophozoites in warm or contaminated water must be introduced through the nose before they can attach to olfactory mucosa and migrate toward the olfactory bulb.
